title: WCSJ 2027 Travel Fellowship: Fully Funded Support for Science Journalists to Attend the World Conference of Science Journalists in London
summary: Applications are now open for the WCSJ 2027 Travel Fellowship , a major international funding opportunity designed to help science journalists, media professionals, journalism students, and eligible researchers or educators attend the World Conference of Science Journalists 2027 in London, United Kingdom . The World Conference of Science Journalists 2027, widely known as WCSJ 2027 , will bring together the global science journalism community in London in September 2027 under the theme: “Strengthening science journalism through global networks.” The conference is hosted by the Association of British Science Writers (ABSW) and the World Federation of Science Journalists (WFSJ) and will provide a global platform for journalists and communicators to exchange ideas, discuss emerging challenges, strengthen professional networks, and examine the future of science journalism. The Travel Fellowship is specifically intended for people who would otherwise struggle to attend because they have limited access to financial support through their employer, organization, institution, or country. Successful applicants may receive support for: International or domestic travel to and from London UK visa application costs Limited local transport connected to the conference Up to six nights of accommodation Full conference registration Refreshments during the conference Lunches provided through the official conference programme The fellowship does not provide a per diem. Applications must be submitted through the official online application form by: 23 October 2026 at 23:59 BST The application process is competitive and international. Applicants are assessed on professional merit, commitment to science journalism, motivation, potential contribution to WCSJ 2027, plans for sharing knowledge afterward, quality of previous journalistic work, and financial need. About the World Conference of Science Journalists 2027 The World Conference of Science Journalists 2027 is one of the most important international gatherings for professionals working at the intersection of journalism, science, health, climate, technology, research, engineering, and public communication. The event will take place in: London, United Kingdom The main conference is announced for: 6–9 September 2027 However, the Travel Fellowship eligibility information asks applicants to be available for the entire fellowship-related conference period from 6–10 September 2027 . Applicants should therefore plan to remain available through 10 September and follow the final schedule provided by WCSJ2027 organizers. The conference theme is: Strengthening science journalism through global networks This theme reflects the increasing importance of international cooperation in a profession facing rapid technological, political, economic, and institutional change. Science journalists today operate in an environment shaped by: Misinformation and disinformation Artificial intelligence Changing media business models Declining newsroom resources Climate change Public-health emergencies Scientific uncertainty Political polarization New digital platforms Trust in science Unequal access to reliable scientific information WCSJ 2027 is intended to provide a space where journalists and related professionals can collectively discuss these challenges and strengthen networks capable of supporting high-quality, independent science journalism. About the WCSJ 2027 Travel Fellowship The Travel Fellowship was created to broaden access to WCSJ 2027. It recognizes that many excellent journalists, journalism students, and media professionals cannot attend major international conferences because their organizations or institutions do not have sufficient travel budgets. This can particularly affect professionals working in: Low-income countries Lower-middle-income countries Small independent media organizations Freelance journalism Underfunded newsrooms Universities with limited travel funding Emerging science journalism communities The Fellowship therefore aims to increase: International participation Diversity Geographic representation Professional access Inclusion of people with limited funding opportunities It is not restricted only to people whose job title is “science journalist.” Applicants may qualify if journalism forms a meaningful part of their professional or academic work. What the WCSJ 2027 Travel Fellowship Covers Successful applicants receive a financial support package intended to make conference participation possible. 1. Travel to and From London Approved travel may include transportation such as: Plane Train Coach Bus WCSJ2027 Ltd will arrange and pay for approved travel directly. Applicants should not assume they will simply receive a lump-sum travel payment. The organizers will generally book approved transport and accommodation on behalf of successful fellows. 2. Visa Application Costs The fellowship can support the cost of applying for a: UK Standard Visitor visa where one is required. Applicants should check their visa requirements before applying. They are specifically advised to use official UK government resources to determine whether they need a visa. Applicants who require a visa should also consider the processing time involved and ensure that they can meet all required documentation and travel conditions. 3. Limited Local Transport The Travel Fellowship may support local transport associated with attending the conference. Examples may include transfers between: Airport and conference-related accommodation Railway station and accommodation Bus station and accommodation Main conference venue Workshop venues Official conference evening events where applicable However, general local transportation in London that is unrelated to official conference activities is not automatically covered. 4. Accommodation The fellowship includes: Up to six nights of accommodation Accommodation is expected to be booked directly by WCSJ2027 Ltd. Applicants should not assume they can independently book additional hotel nights and request reimbursement. Extra nights outside the approved fellowship period are not covered. 5. Full Conference Registration Successful Travel Fellows receive: Full WCSJ 2027 conference registration This provides access to the official conference programme and professional activities. 6. Refreshments and Lunches The fellowship includes: Refreshments during the official conference programme Lunches provided through the conference programme However, meals outside the official conference schedule are not generally covered. What the Fellowship Does Not Cover Applicants should carefully understand the costs that remain their own responsibility. The Travel Fellowship does not cover : General local transport in London unrelated to official venues or activities Local transport in the applicant’s home country Travel undertaken to obtain or renew a passport Travel undertaken to apply for a visa Additional hotel nights not booked by WCSJ2027 Charges added personally to a hotel room Meals outside the official conference programme Personal expenses Travel insurance Health expenses Per diem payments This distinction is important when preparing the funding statement. Applicants should think realistically about whether they can cover expenses that fall outside the fellowship package. Who Can Apply? The fellowship is open to several categories of applicants. 1. Science Journalists and Other Media Professionals Journalists who cover science or science-related subjects are eligible. Relevant areas include: Science Engineering Climate Health Environment Medicine Technology Research Related scientific fields Importantly, science journalism does not have to be the applicant’s primary profession or full-time beat . A journalist who regularly covers health, climate, engineering, science policy, or other scientific subjects as part of a broader reporting role may qualify. Eligible professionals may include: Staff journalists Freelance journalists Part-time journalists Full-time journalists Print journalists Online journalists Broadcast journalists Podcast journalists Multimedia journalists Producers Editors Other media professionals with a journalism track record 2. Journalism and Related Students Students may also apply. Relevant fields include: Science journalism Journalism Media studies Science communication Related disciplines Students must: Be of legal age in their home country Be able to travel independently Students should provide journalistic work where possible. If they do not have enough published work, supervised long-form coursework may be accepted under certain conditions. 3. Researchers and Educators With Journalism Experience Researchers and educators working in fields such as: Journalism Media studies Science communication may also qualify. However, they must demonstrate a proven track record in journalism . A researcher or lecturer who works only in academic research, teaching, science communication, or public relations and has no professional journalistic involvement is not eligible. This distinction is central to the fellowship. Who Is Not Eligible? Applicants are not eligible if they work exclusively in areas such as: Public relations Science communication Research Teaching without a demonstrated professional involvement in journalism. In other words, a person can be a science communicator, researcher, teacher, or academic and still qualify, but they must show that journalism is genuinely part of their work. Applicants should be able to provide published journalistic work or, where applicable for students, acceptable supervised coursework. No Minimum Professional Experience Requirement There is: No minimum number of years of professional experience Applicants may therefore include both relatively early-career professionals and experienced journalists. The application asks about years of experience primarily for contextual and statistical purposes rather than imposing a minimum threshold. Previous Conference Attendance Applicants who have attended the World Conference of Science Journalists before may still apply. However, previous attendance may be used as a tie-breaker where candidates receive otherwise similar scores. Similarly, applicants who previously received travel fellowship support may still apply, although that previous support may also be considered in a tie-breaking situation. Geographic Eligibility There are: No formal geographic quotas The programme seeks a globally diverse and internationally representative cohort. Applicants may therefore potentially come from any country if they meet the professional and application requirements. However, geographic background can influence the administrative review because WCSJ2027 wants to increase access for professionals with limited funding opportunities. Applicants’ countries of residence will be considered using the World Bank country income classifications in effect on the application deadline. Applicants normally based in countries classified as: Low-income Lower-middle-income will receive additional consideration. This does not mean applicants from upper-middle-income or high-income countries are automatically excluded. Financial need and access to institutional support remain important considerations. The Importance of Financial Need Financial need is a central component of the Travel Fellowship. Applicants will be asked to explain: What funding is already available to them Whether their employer can contribute Whether their institution can contribute Whether another grant supports them Why additional WCSJ2027 funding is necessary Whether they would be unable to attend without fellowship support Applicants should be transparent. Having access to some partial funding does not necessarily disqualify an applicant. Candidates can explain what resources they already have and what gap remains. Passport Requirements Before applying, candidates should ensure that they: Already hold a passport valid until at least the end of September 2027, or Have already applied for a new or renewed passport and can provide evidence of that application Applicants should not wait until selection to begin thinking about travel documents. The fellowship will not pay for travel undertaken specifically to request or obtain a passport. UK Visa Requirements Applicants should determine whether they need a UK Standard Visitor visa . Visa eligibility and requirements vary by nationality. The programme directs candidates to official UK government sources. Applicants who require a visa should make sure they can satisfy requirements in time for the September 2027 conference. The fellowship may cover approved visa application costs but does not cover travel undertaken to attend a visa appointment. English Language Requirement The conference language is: English Applicants do not need to be native speakers. They should, however, be able to: Understand the main points of presentations Participate in professional discussions Communicate with other attendees Benefit from conference sessions The application itself must also be completed in English. Applicants’ English is not expected to be perfect. The organizers specifically emphasize that professional merit and content are more important than native-level English fluency. Application Materials Applicants will need to submit several pieces of professional and supporting information. 1. Current Professional Information Applicants will provide details including: Current employer Institution Professional affiliation Current position Professional role Years of professional experience This information helps reviewers understand the applicant’s professional context. 2. CV or Résumé Applicants must submit a: Maximum two-page CV or résumé The document should focus on information most relevant to: Journalism Science reporting Media work Professional development Science communication where connected to journalism Awards Training Professional associations Relevant publications or projects Because the limit is only two pages, applicants should prioritize carefully. 3. Professional Biography Applicants must provide a professional biography. This should present a concise overview of the candidate’s: Work Areas of expertise Professional interests Journalism background Geographic or thematic focus The biography must be written in English. 4. Published Work Examples Applicants will provide examples of professional work from the: Past two years Accepted work may include: Written journalism Audio journalism Video journalism Multimedia work The quality of these examples is an important selection criterion. Applicants should therefore choose pieces that best demonstrate: Accuracy Independence Critical thinking Reporting ability Quality of storytelling Scientific understanding Public relevance Three Work Examples and Quality Assessment The selection criteria state that the quality of professional work is assessed primarily through the: Three work examples provided Applicants should therefore treat these selections strategically. Choose work that demonstrates your strongest journalism rather than simply the most recent pieces. Work in Languages Other Than English Applicants may submit journalistic work originally published in another language. They should provide: The original work An English translation or transcript A link to the original publication where possible AI-assisted translation is allowed. However, the translation must remain faithful to the original work. The original should also be provided so multilingual reviewers can assess it where possible. English proficiency will not be used to downgrade the professional quality of work originally created in another language. Accepted File Formats Professional work may be supplied in formats such as: PDF MP3 MP4 JPEG PNG Applicants should also provide links to original publications whenever possible. Co-Authored Work Co-authored or collaboratively produced work may be submitted. However, applicants should: Be clearly identified as an author, or Clearly explain their contribution This enables reviewers to assess the candidate’s individual professional contribution. Unpublished Work Media professionals generally cannot submit unpublished work as professional work examples. Students are treated somewhat differently. Students should submit published work whenever possible, including content from: University newspapers Student radio Blogs Other published student media If a student cannot provide enough published work, supervised long-form coursework may be submitted, provided it is accompanied by confirmation from the teacher who supervised it. Supporting Letter Applicants must provide a supporting letter from an appropriate professional or institutional source. This may come from: Employer Editor Educational institution Relevant professional association The supporting letter must be: Written in English, or Accompanied by an English translation If translated, the translation should be approved by the original author. The person providing the letter should also read the WCSJ2027 Travel Fellowship Privacy Notice because their personal and professional information may be processed during the application review. Professional Questions in the Application Applicants must answer several substantive questions. These answers are a critical part of the selection process. Why Do You Want to Attend WCSJ2027? Applicants should explain specifically why this conference matters to their professional development. Avoid generic answers such as: “I want to network and learn new things.” A stronger response should connect the WCSJ programme and international community to the applicant’s real professional goals. What Do You Hope to Learn? Applicants should identify concrete skills, knowledge, or professional insights they hope to gain. Potential areas may include: Reporting methods Investigative techniques Covering emerging technologies Climate reporting Health journalism Scientific misinformation Data journalism Audience engagement Editorial innovation The best answer will be specific to the applicant. How Will Attendance Benefit Your Professional Work? Applicants should explain how knowledge gained at WCSJ2027 could improve: Reporting Editing Teaching Professional networks Newsroom practices Coverage quality Professional leadership The reviewers are looking for evidence that the fellowship will have an impact beyond a single international trip. What Will You Contribute? The conference seeks participants who contribute to the community rather than only receive benefits. Applicants should consider what they bring through: Regional expertise Professional experience Language skills Specialized reporting Knowledge of local media environments Training experience Community leadership Underrepresented perspectives How Will You Share What You Learn? Applicants need to explain how conference knowledge will be shared afterward. Possible approaches could include: Training colleagues Writing articles Hosting newsroom sessions Organizing workshops Sharing resources through professional associations Mentoring younger journalists Publishing conference reflections Building local networks The strongest plans will be realistic and directly connected to existing professional communities. Funding Statement Applicants must provide a funding statement explaining: Current available support Funding gaps Why additional financial support is required This is central to assessing need. Reviewers handling professional merit will not necessarily have access to this financial information. Selection Process Applications undergo a: Two-stage assessment Stage 1: Professional Review Professional reviewers assess areas including: Quality of journalism Professional experience Motivation Commitment to science journalism Potential contribution to WCSJ2027 Professional-development potential Stage 2: Administrative and Eligibility Review Authorized WCSJ2027 Travel Fellowship administrators assess: Eligibility Administrative completeness Financial need Programme objectives Overall geographic and professional composition of the cohort This process helps the organizers balance professional merit with the fellowship’s goal of broadening access. Selection Criteria Applications are evaluated against several published criteria. Commitment to Science Journalism Applicants should demonstrate engagement with: Accurate journalism Fair journalism Critical journalism Independent journalism This can be shown through reporting, editorial work, professional activities, or broader contributions to science journalism. Professional Development and Community Engagement The reviewers will consider involvement in activities such as: Professional associations Journalist networks Training Teaching Mentoring Science journalism communities Participation is not necessarily limited to formal organizations. Motivation Applicants should explain convincingly why WCSJ2027 specifically matters to their career. Reviewers are looking for a well-expressed and engaging motivation rather than generic conference interest. Potential Benefit and Contribution The application should demonstrate both: What the applicant will gain What the applicant will contribute This reciprocal approach is central to the fellowship. Sharing the Benefits Applicants should have a credible plan to extend the impact of their participation to others. Reviewers will consider how knowledge might reach: Colleagues Professional networks Students Audiences Regional journalism communities Quality of Professional Work Professional quality is assessed primarily through the submitted work examples. Applicants should select their strongest work carefully. Financial Need The programme specifically exists for candidates who would otherwise have difficulty attending. Reviewers will therefore consider financial circumstances as an essential part of final funding decisions. Diversity and International Representation WCSJ2027 seeks a cohort that is: Diverse International Professionally varied Geographically representative No geographic quotas are used. However, geographic representation and limited funding opportunities may influence final cohort composition. Privacy and Fair Assessment Applicants must read the official WCSJ2027 Travel Fellowship Privacy Notice before submitting. The notice explains: How personal data will be used Applicant privacy rights Data-processing safeguards Selection procedures Reviewers are also subject to an official agreement covering: Confidentiality Conflict of interest Fair assessment Professional reviewers receive only the information required to assess merit. They do not receive access to information such as: Passport details Contact information Funding statements This separation is intended to support impartial assessment. Online Application Only Applications must be submitted through the official online form , The organizers also provide an offline downloadable version of the form. However, the offline document is only intended to help applicants prepare responses. It cannot be submitted as the final application . Saving and Returning to Your Application The application takes approximately: 30 minutes Applicants do not necessarily have to complete it in one sitting. The form allows candidates to save their progress and return later. Applicants may need to hover near the left side of the “Next” button to reveal the “Save” option. Can You Correct an Application After Submission? Yes. Before the deadline, candidates can either: Submit a new application, or Contact the organizers If multiple applications are submitted, only the: Most recent application will be considered. Questions can be directed to: info@absw.org.uk Required Fields Are Important Applicants must provide all information marked with a red asterisk. If necessary information or supporting documentation is missing and reviewers cannot assess eligibility or professional merit, the application may be excluded. Candidates should therefore conduct a complete final check before submission. AI Use in Applications WCSJ2027 permits AI tools for a very limited purpose: Translation or transcription of professional work originally published in another language. The translation must remain faithful to the original. However, applicants are expected to write their own: Professional biography Motivation statement Knowledge-sharing plan Funding statement Other personal application responses The organizers explicitly state that they do not expect perfect English. Answers are evaluated primarily for substance rather than native-level language ability. Key Dates Applications open: 2026 Travel Fellowship deadline: October 23, 2026 at 23:59 BST Conference: September 6–9, 2027 Travel Fellowship attendance requirement: Applicants should be available September 6–10, 2027 Location: London, United Kingdom Important Pre-Application Checklist Before submitting, applicants should confirm that they: Meet one of the eligible professional or student categories. Have journalism as part of their professional work, unless applying under the student provisions. Can attend the entire required conference period. Have or are applying for an appropriate passport. Have checked whether they require a UK visa. Can complete the application in English. Have prepared a two-page CV. Have selected three strong work examples. Have obtained a supporting letter. Have prepared a clear funding statement. Have a credible plan to share knowledge after the conference. Tips for Preparing a Competitive WCSJ2027 Travel Fellowship Application 1. Choose Your Three Strongest Journalism Examples Do not automatically submit your three newest pieces. Choose work that shows: Strong reporting Critical thinking Clear communication Scientific complexity handled accurately Independent journalism Public relevance 2. Make Your Motivation Specific to WCSJ2027 Read about the conference theme and consider why a global science journalism network matters to your work. Explain why this particular conference, rather than any generic journalism event, is important. 3. Demonstrate Community Impact If you already contribute to: Journalism associations Training Mentorship Newsroom development Student journalism Professional networks explain this clearly. It can show that the fellowship’s impact will extend beyond you. 4. Be Concrete About Knowledge Sharing Instead of saying: “I will share what I learn with colleagues,” describe exactly how. For example: A newsroom workshop Regional webinar Training session Professional association briefing Journalism article Mentoring programme 5. Be Transparent About Financial Need The fellowship exists specifically to improve access. Explain the financial barriers honestly. If you have partial support, mention it and explain what gap remains. 6. Explain What You Bring to the Global Community Your professional background, geography, language, expertise, or reporting experience may provide insights others do not have. Explain that contribution confidently and specifically. 7. Do Not Ignore Travel Readiness Passport and visa readiness are important. Make sure you can realistically travel to London in September 2027 if selected. Why the WCSJ 2027 Travel Fellowship Matters Major international conferences can shape careers by giving journalists access to: New reporting methods Professional networks Mentors Editors Collaborators Training opportunities International perspectives Yet access to these conferences remains unequal. Journalists in countries or institutions with limited travel funding may have fewer opportunities to participate in international professional networks despite producing high-quality work. The WCSJ 2027 Travel Fellowship seeks to reduce this inequality by supporting people whose professional contribution and potential are strong but whose financial resources are limited. Conclusion The WCSJ 2027 Travel Fellowship is an important international opportunity for science journalists, media professionals, journalism students, and eligible researchers or educators who want to participate in the World Conference of Science Journalists 2027 in London but would otherwise be unable to afford the associated costs. Successful applicants may receive support covering approved travel, visa application costs, limited local transportation, up to six nights of accommodation, full conference registration, refreshments, and official conference lunches. The fellowship does not provide per diem payments and does not cover personal expenses, travel insurance, health expenses, additional hotel nights, or unrelated local transport. The opportunity is open internationally and does not impose geographic quotas. Applicants from countries classified by the World Bank as low-income or lower-middle-income will receive additional consideration as part of the programme’s commitment to broader global participation. Eligible applicants include journalists and media professionals covering science and related subjects, students in journalism and related fields, and researchers or educators with a proven professional journalism track record. Applicants must submit a two-page CV, professional biography, examples of recent journalistic work, a supporting letter, professional-development responses, a knowledge-sharing plan, and a financial-needs statement. Applications are assessed through a competitive two-stage international process based on professional merit, science-journalism commitment, motivation, professional contribution, quality of work, knowledge-sharing potential, and financial need. The application deadline is: 23 October 2026 at 23:59 BST The conference will take place in London in September 2027 under the theme: “Strengthening science journalism through global networks.” To know more information about this opportunity, VISIT HERE . title: University of the Witwatersrand PhD and LLM Bursaries 2027: Up to R200,000 for African Law Researchers
summary: Applications are open for the 2027 PhD and LLM by Research bursaries at the University of the Witwatersrand School of Law , offering postgraduate funding for researchers interested in equality, socio-economic rights, land rights, housing, social justice, and African human rights law. The bursaries are offered through the NRF-funded South African Research Chair in Equality, Law and Social Justice , based at the School of Law, University of the Witwatersrand (Wits University), Johannesburg, South Africa . Successful applicants will undertake either a PhD or an LLM by Research beginning in 2027 under the supervision of the Chair or associated academics. The opportunity is particularly significant for postgraduate researchers from South Africa and other African countries whose proposed research aligns with one of the Chair’s identified areas of interest. For 2027, the bursary value is approximately: R200,000 for PhD candidates who qualify for the higher level of NRF support R190,000 for LLM candidates who qualify for the higher level of NRF support Approximately R150,000 for PhD candidates qualifying at the lower funding level Approximately R145,000 for LLM candidates qualifying at the lower funding level The higher funding level is linked to the NRF’s means-tested funding provisions or applicants with academic averages of 75% or higher , while students with a minimum academic average of 65% may qualify for partial bursary amounts. Applicants must study full-time at Wits University , meet the relevant academic and age requirements, and successfully complete several stages of approval involving the SARChI Chair, the National Research Foundation, and the Wits School of Law. The application deadline is 30 September 2026 . About the Wits University School of Law Postgraduate Funding Opportunity The funding opportunity is offered through the South African Research Chair in Equality, Law and Social Justice , commonly referred to as a SARChI Chair. The Chair is supported by the National Research Foundation of South Africa (NRF) and is hosted within the School of Law at the University of the Witwatersrand. The 2027 call seeks postgraduate researchers who want to undertake sustained research on questions related to: Equality Law Social justice Socio-economic rights Land rights Housing Vulnerable groups African regional institutions African human rights mechanisms The funding is available for two research-degree routes: PhD LLM by Research Applicants should therefore be interested in completing an advanced research degree rather than a coursework-only programme. Research Areas Available for 2027 Applicants must propose research that fits within one of the areas identified by the SARChI Chair. The five research areas are: Intergenerational equity and women’s land rights Impact of intergenerational injustice on the right to housing Contributions of African regional bodies to the development and enforcement of economic, social and cultural rights The role of economic, social and cultural rights in addressing inequalities among vulnerable groups in Africa Advancing equality and social change through the African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights These research areas place the opportunity firmly within broader debates about law, justice, rights, inequality, and African legal institutions. 1. Intergenerational Equity and Women’s Land Rights One of the research areas concerns: Intergenerational equity and women’s land rights. Applicants interested in this field would need to develop a research question addressing the relationship between gender, land rights, justice across generations, and relevant legal frameworks. The call itself does not prescribe a specific research question, country case study, legal jurisdiction, or methodology. Applicants therefore need to formulate their own focused research problem within this broader theme. The one-to-two-page summary research proposal required at the initial application stage should clearly identify the legal or socio-legal issue the candidate intends to investigate. 2. Intergenerational Injustice and the Right to Housing A second research area is: The impact of intergenerational injustice on the right to housing. This theme connects questions of historical or inherited inequality with legal protections concerning housing. Applicants should propose a clearly defined research problem rather than merely stating that they want to research housing rights. The Chair is looking for a concise proposal demonstrating that the candidate has identified a substantive question appropriate for advanced postgraduate research. 3. African Regional Bodies and Economic, Social and Cultural Rights The third research area focuses on: The contributions of African regional bodies to the development and enforcement of economic, social and cultural rights. Economic, social and cultural rights are often abbreviated as ESC rights . This research area is particularly relevant to candidates interested in African regional human rights law and institutions. The call does not prescribe which regional body, particular right, or country should form the focus of the research, so applicants will need to define an appropriate research scope themselves. 4. ESC Rights and Inequality Among Vulnerable Groups in Africa Another priority is: The role of economic, social and cultural rights in addressing inequalities among vulnerable groups in Africa. This theme combines: Rights Inequality Social justice Vulnerability African legal and policy contexts Applicants will need to identify which rights, groups, legal frameworks, or inequalities their proposed study will address. The research should remain closely aligned with the broader work of the Chair in Equality, Law and Social Justice. 5. African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights, Equality and Social Change The fifth research area concerns: Advancing equality and social change through the African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights. This provides a particularly strong avenue for applicants interested in: African human rights law Regional judicial institutions Equality Rights enforcement Legal approaches to social change Again, the call identifies the broad research field rather than providing a predetermined dissertation project. Candidates are expected to formulate their own viable research question. Degree Options The funding opportunity supports two postgraduate research degrees. PhD Applicants may apply to undertake a doctoral degree under the supervision of the SARChI Chair or associated scholars. The PhD bursary may provide approximately: R200,000 for candidates meeting the applicable higher-level NRF funding criteria. For applicants with the minimum qualifying academic average of 65%, the funding may instead be approximately: R150,000 or the applicable part thereof. LLM by Research The opportunity also supports candidates undertaking an: LLM by Research This is distinct from a coursework-based LLM. The LLM by Research bursary may be approximately: R190,000 for applicants qualifying for the higher NRF funding level. For candidates with a minimum academic average of 65%, the amount may be approximately: R145,000 or part thereof. Understanding the 2027 Bursary Amounts Applicants should pay close attention to the way the funding is structured. The call states that the approximate 2027 NRF bursary values are: Higher funding level PhD: Approximately R200,000 LLM: Approximately R190,000 This higher level applies under the relevant NRF means-tested funding criteria or for students with academic averages of: 75% or higher Lower or partial funding level Applicants meeting the minimum average of: 65% may qualify for approximately: R150,000 for PhD or: R145,000 for LLM or the applicable part thereof. Applicants should therefore not assume that every successful candidate automatically receives the maximum stated amount. Actual funding is subject to NRF eligibility and approval. The Bursary Must Be the Primary Funding The call states that the NRF bursary should be held as the applicant’s: Primary funding towards the degree. Candidates who already have another major funding source should therefore consult the relevant NRF rules to determine whether the funding can be combined with other awards. The detailed NRF Postgraduate Funding Framework should be reviewed carefully by applicants who have questions about concurrent funding or other financial conditions. Who Can Apply? Applicants must meet several important requirements. They must: Intend to undertake either a PhD or LLM by Research Study full-time Study at the University of the Witwatersrand Work under the supervision of the Chair or associates Be South African or come from another African country Meet the required minimum academic average Meet the NRF age requirement Submit a research proposal aligned with one of the five listed areas This is therefore a targeted postgraduate research funding opportunity rather than a general scholarship open to all programmes at Wits University. Full-Time Study Requirement Successful applicants must undertake their degree: Full-time at: Wits University The funding is therefore not presented as support for part-time postgraduate study. Applicants should be prepared to commit to the academic requirements of a full-time research programme. Academic Requirements The call specifies a minimum academic average of: 65% in the applicant’s previous degree The qualifying previous degree is generally: LLB for relevant LLM applicants LLM for PhD applicants The 65% threshold is the minimum requirement for NRF bursary eligibility under this opportunity. Applicants with academic averages of 75% or above may potentially qualify for the higher funding level identified in the call. Age Requirements The NRF funding also includes maximum age requirements. LLM Applicants Applicants must be: 30 years old or younger in 2027 The announcement states that candidates must not be older than 30 in 2027. PhD Applicants Applicants must be: 32 years old or younger in 2027 Candidates must therefore not be older than 32 in 2027. These are important eligibility conditions. A strong academic record does not override the age requirements stated for the NRF bursary. Nationality and Geographic Eligibility The opportunity is open to: South African applicants Applicants from other African countries This makes the bursary a continentally accessible postgraduate opportunity rather than one restricted only to South African nationals. Applicants from African countries outside South Africa must still meet all academic, programme, funding, and admission requirements. Required Application Documents Applicants must prepare six main components. 1. Covering Letter Candidates must submit a letter explaining: Why they are interested in the bursary. The letter should therefore be tailored specifically to the SARChI Chair opportunity. A strong covering letter should connect: The applicant’s academic background Research interests Proposed topic Interest in equality, law and social justice Long-term academic or professional goals Reasons for wanting to work with the Chair Candidates should avoid sending a generic postgraduate funding letter. 2. One-to-Two-Page Research Proposal Applicants must provide a: One-to-two-page summary research proposal The proposal should clearly specify: The issue the applicant wishes to research. This is one of the most important components of the application. Because the proposal is short, candidates need to present their idea concisely. A useful structure may include: Proposed title Research problem Main research question Brief background Relevance to one of the Chair’s research areas Proposed legal or research approach Expected contribution Applicants should remain within the required one-to-two-page length. Choosing a Research Topic The research proposal should align directly with one of the five announced areas. Candidates should avoid proposing a broad topic such as: “Human rights in Africa” or: “Women’s rights.” Instead, the proposal should identify a specific and researchable legal issue. The application should make clear why the project belongs within the Chair’s programme on: Equality, Law and Social Justice. 3. Copy of ID or Passport Applicants must provide either: Identification document, or Passport This helps establish identity and relevant nationality information. International African applicants should ensure their passport documentation is clear and valid. 4. Curriculum Vitae Applicants must submit an updated CV. For an academic postgraduate funding application, the CV should highlight information such as: Education Academic results Research experience Dissertation or thesis experience Publications, if any Research assistant work Mooting or legal research Internships Relevant professional experience Awards Conferences Teaching or tutoring Community or public-interest work Candidates should prioritize experiences connected to law, rights, equality, social justice, or their proposed research field. 5. Full Academic Records Applicants must provide: Full academic records This is essential because the NRF bursary has explicit minimum academic thresholds. Candidates should ensure the submitted record clearly demonstrates their academic performance. 6. Two Academic Referees Applicants must provide: Contact details for two academic referees. Referees should ideally be academics who know the applicant’s research or academic abilities well. Potential referees might include: Thesis supervisor Dissertation supervisor Research project supervisor Lecturer Professor familiar with the applicant’s work The announcement asks for contact details rather than stating that recommendation letters must be submitted with the initial application. Applicants should follow any subsequent instructions they receive from the Chair. Application Process: Three Important Stages Applicants should understand that acceptance by the SARChI Chair is not the final funding decision . The process involves multiple stages. Stage 1: Apply to the SARChI Chair Applicants first submit the required documents to the Chair’s application contact. The application will be evaluated for: Research alignment Academic eligibility Bursary criteria Suitability for supervision Stage 2: Apply to the NRF Candidates accepted by the Chair will subsequently need to submit an application through the: National Research Foundation online system Acceptance by the Chair remains subject to NRF approval. The SARChI Chair will provide additional details to candidates who reach this stage. Stage 3: Apply to the Wits School of Law Successful bursary candidates must also obtain admission to the appropriate: Wits School of Law programme This means that being selected for consideration by the Chair does not automatically constitute formal admission to Wits University. Candidates must successfully satisfy the academic admission requirements for the relevant: PhD, or LLM by Research programme. Important Conditional Nature of the Award Applicants should therefore understand that final funding depends on: Acceptance by the SARChI Chair NRF approval Successful admission to the relevant Wits School of Law programme All three elements matter. How to Submit the Application Applications must be sent to: Judy Mafika Email: judy.mafika@wits.ac.za Candidates are encouraged to submit: As soon as possible and no later than: 30 September 2026 Late applications will not be considered. Incomplete applications will also not be considered. Applicants should therefore confirm that all required documents are attached before sending their application. Application Deadline The final deadline is: 30 September 2026 This is the deadline for the initial application to the SARChI Chair. Applicants should not confuse this deadline with later NRF or Wits University processes that may apply after selection. When Will Applicants Hear Back? The announcement states that applicants who do not receive communication by: The end of October 2026 should consider their application to the Chair unsuccessful. This provides candidates with a relatively clear timeline for the first stage of the process. Enquiries About Research Scope Applicants who have questions about the research areas or whether their proposed project fits the Chair’s programme may contact: Professor Cathi Albertyn cathi.albertyn@wits.ac.za or: Professor Lilian Chenwi lilian.chenwi@wits.ac.za Questions concerning the scope of the research area or bursary criteria should be directed to these contacts. About the SARChI Chair in Equality, Law and Social Justice The postgraduate bursaries are connected to the: South African Research Chair in Equality, Law and Social Justice at the University of the Witwatersrand. The Chair’s 2027 research themes show a strong focus on the relationship between law and structural inequality. Across the five identified areas, recurring themes include: Equality Intergenerational justice Women’s rights Land rights Housing Economic, social and cultural rights Vulnerable groups African institutions Regional human rights law Social change This makes the bursary particularly relevant to students interested in legal research that examines how law interacts with inequality and social transformation. Why the Opportunity Is Particularly Relevant to African Researchers The programme explicitly welcomes candidates from: South Africa and other African countries. Research topics are also heavily centered on African legal and human rights questions. This combination provides opportunities for researchers to examine legal issues within African contexts while being based at a major South African university. The identified themes encourage research relating to: African rights institutions African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights Vulnerable groups in Africa Regional approaches to ESC rights Equality and social justice Understanding ESC Rights Several of the research themes refer to: ESC rights This stands for: Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. Within the context of this call, applicants may be interested in examining how legal frameworks and institutions contribute to developing, enforcing, or using such rights to respond to inequality. The specific right, jurisdiction, population, or institutional focus must be defined by the applicant’s proposal. Preparing a Competitive Application 1. Start With the Research Fit The first question applicants should ask is not: “How much funding can I receive?” Instead, ask: “Does my research genuinely fit one of the five themes?” Strong thematic alignment is fundamental. 2. Make the Research Problem Specific A one-to-two-page proposal does not allow space for an extremely broad topic. Clearly state: What problem exists What legal question you want to answer Why the question matters Where the research is situated What contribution the project could make 3. Connect the Project to Equality and Social Justice Even when choosing a specific area such as land, housing, or the African Court, applicants should make the connection with the Chair’s overarching concern with: Equality, Law and Social Justice clear. 4. Demonstrate Academic Readiness The minimum average is 65%, but a competitive application should communicate more than numerical eligibility. Candidates can highlight: Strong legal research Previous dissertation work Research methods Academic writing Relevant coursework Publications Conference work where applicable. 5. Choose Strong Academic Referees Your referees should be capable of discussing your ability to undertake independent postgraduate research. A famous academic who barely knows your work may be less useful than a lecturer or supervisor familiar with your academic strengths. 6. Check the Age Requirement Before Applying The age limits are explicit: LLM: maximum 30 in 2027 PhD: maximum 32 in 2027 Applicants should verify this condition before investing substantial time in preparing the application. 7. Submit a Complete Application The call states explicitly: Incomplete applications will not be considered. Before submitting, check that your application contains: Covering letter Research proposal ID/passport CV Full academic records Two academic referees Application Checklist Before sending your application, confirm that you have: Written a tailored covering letter. Prepared a one-to-two-page research proposal. Selected one of the five relevant research areas. Included your ID or passport. Updated your CV. Attached full academic records. Provided two academic referee contacts. Checked that your previous-degree average is at least 65%. Confirmed that you meet the NRF age requirement. Confirmed that you can study full-time at Wits University. Confirmed that you are South African or from another African country. Submitted everything by September 30, 2026. Important Dates at a Glance Opportunity announced: 20 August 2026 Application deadline: 30 September 2026 Initial outcome timeframe: By the end of October 2026 Study commencement: 2027 Applicants accepted by the Chair will subsequently receive information concerning their NRF and Wits School of Law applications. Important Funding Details at a Glance PhD Higher-level bursary: Approximately R200,000 Other qualifying funding level: Approximately R150,000 or part thereof LLM by Research Higher-level bursary: Approximately R190,000 Other qualifying funding level: Approximately R145,000 or part thereof Academic threshold Minimum: 65% Applicants with: 75% or higher may be eligible for the higher stated funding level, alongside the applicable means-tested criteria. Important Eligibility Details at a Glance University: University of the Witwatersrand School: Wits School of Law Research Chair: NRF SARChI Chair in Equality, Law and Social Justice Degrees: PhD or LLM by Research Study mode: Full-time Location: Johannesburg, South Africa Eligible applicants: South Africans and applicants from other African countries Minimum academic average: 65% Maximum age for LLM: 30 in 2027 Maximum age for PhD: 32 in 2027 Deadline: 30 September 2026 Conclusion The University of the Witwatersrand PhD and LLM Bursaries 2027 provide an important postgraduate funding opportunity for African researchers interested in law, equality, socio-economic rights and social justice. Offered through the NRF-funded SARChI Chair in Equality, Law and Social Justice at Wits School of Law , the opportunity supports full-time PhD and LLM by Research candidates working in one of five areas: Intergenerational equity and women’s land rights Intergenerational injustice and housing rights African regional bodies and economic, social and cultural rights ESC rights and inequalities affecting vulnerable groups in Africa Equality and social change through the African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights The approximate 2027 funding can reach R200,000 for PhD candidates and R190,000 for LLM candidates under the applicable higher funding criteria, while other candidates meeting the minimum 65% academic requirement may qualify for approximately R150,000 or R145,000 respectively, or part thereof. Candidates must be South African or from another African country, study full-time at Wits University, meet the applicable NRF academic and age criteria, and conduct their research under the Chair or associated supervisors. Applicants need to submit a covering letter, one-to-two-page research proposal, ID or passport, CV, full academic records and details of two academic referees. Initial acceptance by the Chair remains subject to both NRF approval and successful admission to the appropriate Wits School of Law programme . The deadline for applications is 30 September 2026 . For further information, applicants can consult the Wits University announcement and the NRF Postgraduate Funding Framework or contact Professors Cathi Albertyn and Lilian Chenwi regarding research scope and bursary criteria. title: UN Women HeForShe Barbershop Facilitator Consultant Roster: Remote Consultancy Opportunity for Gender Equality Experts
summary: Professionals with expertise in gender equality, equitable masculinities, male allyship, social norm change, human rights, training and community engagement can explore a consultancy opportunity with UN Women through the HeForShe Barbershop Facilitator Consultant Roster . The opportunity is designed to establish a pool of qualified and pre-vetted facilitators who can support the delivery and contextual adaptation of the HeForShe Barbershop Toolkit across different countries, languages and communities. The consultancy is home-based and primarily remote , although selected consultants may be required to undertake short-term in-person facilitation assignments or field missions depending on programme requirements. Unlike a conventional full-time employment position, inclusion in the consultant roster does not guarantee an immediate assignment. Instead, successful candidates become part of a pre-vetted pool that UN Women can draw upon when programmes, country offices, regional offices or implementing partners require qualified Barbershop facilitators. About UN Women UN Women is the United Nations entity dedicated to gender equality and the empowerment of women. The organization works toward the elimination of discrimination against women and girls, the empowerment of women, and the achievement of equality between women and men as partners and beneficiaries of development, human rights, humanitarian action, and peace and security. The Barbershop Facilitator opportunity sits within UN Women s Strategic Partnerships Division , specifically the Private Sector Partnerships Section . The Private Sector Partnerships Section leads UN Women s engagement with: Private-sector organizations Corporations Philanthropic organizations Foundations Individuals The section also supports and drives several major global initiatives, including: HeForShe Women s Empowerment Principles Unstereotype Alliance Its broader objective is to develop and sustain high-quality, impact-focused partnerships that contribute to gender equality and women s empowerment. What Is the HeForShe Barbershop Toolkit? The Barbershop Toolkit is a participatory HeForShe programme designed to engage men and boys in discussions and learning around gender equality, equitable masculinities and social norms. The programme is rooted in the Transforming Patriarchal Masculinities (TPM) approach. Through facilitated discussions, participants can explore how social expectations and norms surrounding masculinity affect individuals, relationships, communities and broader society. The initiative is intended to operate across multiple countries and languages. Because of this, UN Women is seeking qualified facilitators who can not only deliver Barbershop sessions but also help adapt the programme to different local environments and communities. What Is the Consultant Roster? The consultant roster is a mechanism used by UN Women to maintain a pool of pre-vetted experts with particular areas of specialization. The purpose is to make it easier for UN Women headquarters, regional offices and country offices to quickly access qualified expertise when new programmes need to be launched, existing programmes need additional support, or urgent assignments require rapid deployment. For this particular opportunity, successful consultants can potentially be called upon to support Barbershop programming based on demand from UN Women and its implementing partners. However, applicants should understand an important distinction: Being accepted into the consultant roster does not guarantee employment or an assignment. Actual engagements depend on: Programme needs Requests from implementing partners Availability of resources The geographic requirements of a particular assignment The need for specific expertise Consultants are therefore engaged on an as-needed basis , with the duration and frequency of assignments potentially varying over time. Working Arrangement The consultancy is structured as a home-based assignment . Consultants will primarily work remotely and may receive assignments depending on UN Women s programme requirements. However, the work is not necessarily exclusively virtual. Where necessary, consultants may be asked to undertake: Short-term in-person facilitation assignments Field missions National travel International travel Travel requirements will be determined on a case-by-case basis according to the needs of the programme and the location where Barbershop sessions are being implemented. APPLY HERE When Will Barbershop Sessions Begin? The consultant roster onboarding process includes mandatory webinars and preparation activities. The actual Barbershop Toolkit sessions are expected to begin in Q4 2026 . Consultants will report to the Partnerships Engagement and Special Initiatives Advisor and Global Head of HeForShe , who will serve as the focal point for contractual and payment-related matters. Once engaged, consultants are expected to work independently while following the established Barbershop methodology, facilitation standards, implementation protocols and monitoring and evaluation framework. Consultant Responsibilities and Deliverables The consultancy includes several stages, beginning with onboarding and preparation and continuing through session delivery, monitoring, evaluation and knowledge sharing. 1. Complete Mandatory Barbershop Onboarding Consultants must participate in mandatory Barbershop orientation and coordination webinars. They are expected to attend at least 80% of the mandatory webinars organized by UN Women. The purpose of these sessions is to ensure that facilitators understand and can properly apply: Barbershop methodology Facilitation standards Implementation protocols Curriculum objectives Reporting requirements Consultants must also review relevant materials, including: The facilitation toolkit Safeguarding guidance Implementation framework After completing the onboarding process, consultants are expected to confirm their understanding of the curriculum objectives and reporting requirements. The onboarding webinars are envisioned to take place during 2026. Importantly, the supplied information states that the first six months from roster onboarding are not paid activity and that the webinars are not compensated. Consultants may spend up to 10 hours per year participating in mandatory onboarding and knowledge-exchange webinars, with that participation time not compensated. 2. Prepare Adapted Barbershop Session Materials Before delivering sessions, consultants will be responsible for reviewing the standard Barbershop curriculum and adapting the content where necessary. The adaptation process may involve considering: Local language Cultural context Socio-cultural environment Participant profile Specific setting Partner requirements Available logistics The consultant must ensure that adaptations remain aligned with the core objectives and methodology of the Barbershop programme. Consultants will also coordinate with UN Women or the relevant implementing partner to ensure that the session design is appropriate and that all necessary preparations have been completed. The finalized adapted materials must be submitted at least 7 working days before the workshop delivery date . 3. Deliver Barbershop Sessions The central responsibility of the facilitator is to conduct Barbershop sessions with groups of men and boys. Sessions must be delivered according to the standardized curriculum and approved guidelines. Facilitators will be expected to: Conduct Barbershop sessions Facilitate discussions about gender equality Explore equitable masculinities Use the approved curriculum Create a safe and inclusive learning environment Maintain respectful dialogue Adapt facilitation techniques to group dynamics Preserve the core learning objectives of the programme Facilitators must therefore be able to manage group discussions effectively while creating an environment where participants can engage in sensitive conversations in a constructive and respectful manner. 4. Monitoring, Evaluation and Reporting Following each workshop, consultants must complete a structured monitoring and evaluation process. The post-workshop report must align with the Barbershop Monitoring and Evaluation Framework . The report should document: Session delivery Participant attendance Participant engagement Participant profiles Key discussion themes Outcomes Facilitation observations Challenges encountered Lessons learned Recommendations for future sessions Suggested improvements The post-workshop monitoring and evaluation report must be submitted within 5 working days after the workshop has been completed . 5. Contribute to the Barbershop Community of Practice Consultants are also expected to contribute their knowledge and experience to the broader Barbershop community of practice. This can include: Sharing facilitation insights Sharing lessons learned Sharing good practices Participating in community-of-practice platforms Participating in debrief sessions Providing written input for guidance notes Contributing to supplementary facilitation materials Recommending improvements to future Barbershop sessions Providing recommendations for implementation approaches Submitting facilitator testimonials Providing reflective statements for potential use in UN Women communications and advocacy materials This element of the consultancy means that facilitators are not only expected to deliver sessions but can also contribute to improving and strengthening the broader Barbershop initiative. Core Values Expected From Consultants UN Women identifies several core values that consultants are expected to demonstrate. These include: Integrity Professionalism Respect for Diversity These values are particularly relevant to a programme that involves discussions around gender, social norms, identity and cultural contexts. Core Competencies Applicants should also demonstrate a range of professional competencies relevant to facilitation and gender equality programming. These include: Awareness and Sensitivity Regarding Gender Issues Facilitators must understand the sensitive nature of gender-related discussions and be able to engage participants respectfully. Accountability Consultants must take responsibility for delivering agreed activities, meeting deadlines and completing required reporting. Creative Problem Solving Facilitators may encounter different cultural, logistical and group-dynamic challenges and should be able to develop appropriate solutions. Effective Communication Strong communication skills are essential for facilitating discussions and ensuring participants understand the subject matter. Inclusive Collaboration Consultants must be capable of working constructively with UN Women, implementing partners, participants and other stakeholders. Stakeholder Engagement The role requires the ability to engage effectively with different stakeholders involved in programme delivery. Leading by Example Facilitators are expected to demonstrate the principles and professional standards promoted through the programme. Functional Skills and Expertise Required Beyond the general competencies, the consultancy requires specialized knowledge and experience. Applicants should have a strong understanding of: Gender equality Equitable masculinities Social norm change approaches Strong interpersonal, communication and facilitation abilities are also required. Applicants should be capable of: Managing groups Resolving conflicts Facilitating difficult conversations Adapting content to different contexts Working with diverse populations Adjusting content to different literacy levels Working across different languages and cultures Experience in monitoring, evaluation and reporting for training or community-engagement programmes is considered an asset. Knowledge of the UN system and familiarity with intergovernmental processes are also considered assets. Experience with the HeForShe Initiative and Barbershop Toolkit is an additional advantage. Educational Requirements Applicants are generally required to have a Master s degree or equivalent . The preferred fields include: Social Sciences Human Rights Gender Studies Women s Studies International Development Related disciplines However, an alternative pathway is available. A first-level university degree combined with two additional years of qualifying experience may be accepted instead of an advanced university degree. Professional Experience Requirements Applicants must have a minimum of 5 years of work experience . In addition to the general experience requirement, candidates must have experience facilitating: Trainings Workshops Dialogue-based programmes The experience should specifically relate to areas such as: Gender equality Male allyship Equitable masculinities This is an important requirement because the role is not simply an administrative consultancy. Consultants are expected to have the professional experience necessary to lead structured conversations and learning sessions with groups of men and boys. Language Requirements Fluency in written and spoken English is required. Knowledge of an additional language is highly desirable. Additional language skills can be particularly valuable where the facilitator needs to adapt the Barbershop Toolkit and supporting materials to regional or local contexts. UN Women Diversity and Inclusion Commitment UN Women states that it is committed to creating a diverse and inclusive environment based on mutual respect. The organization states that recruitment, employment, training, compensation and promotion are carried out without discrimination based on factors including: Race Religion Colour Sex Gender identity Sexual orientation Age Ability National origin UN Women states that employment decisions are based on qualifications, competence, integrity and organizational need. Candidates who require reasonable accommodation during the recruitment and selection process are encouraged to include that information in their application. Safeguarding and Standards of Conduct UN Women maintains a zero-tolerance policy toward conduct that is incompatible with the aims and objectives of the United Nations and UN Women. This includes: Sexual exploitation and abuse Sexual harassment Abuse of authority Discrimination Selected candidates are expected to comply with UN Women s policies and procedures and the standards of conduct applicable to UN Women personnel. Candidates who are selected may also be subject to rigorous reference and background checks. These checks can include verification of: Academic credentials Employment history Other information required for the recruitment process Selected candidates may be required to provide additional information to complete the background-check process. Important Point About the Consultant Roster Prospective applicants should understand that this is a consultant roster opportunity rather than a guaranteed employment position . Being accepted into the roster means the consultant becomes part of a pool of pre-vetted experts whom UN Women may approach when suitable assignments become available. Actual assignments depend on: Programme demand Partner requests Available funding and resources Required expertise Location and implementation needs Consequently, inclusion in the roster does not automatically mean that a consultant will receive a specific number of assignments or a guaranteed workload. Remote Work and Potential Travel The position is advertised as home-based and remote , making it potentially suitable for qualified professionals who are not based at UN Women offices. However, candidates should be prepared for the possibility of travel. Depending on programme requirements, assignments may involve short-term in-person facilitation or field missions. Travel can potentially be: Within the consultant s country International The exact travel requirements will depend on the assignment and will be determined on a case-by-case basis. Timeline and Key Dates The supplied opportunity information indicates that: Mandatory onboarding webinars are envisioned for 2026 . The first six months from roster onboarding involve onboarding activity that is not paid. Barbershop Toolkit sessions are expected to begin in Q4 2026 . Adapted session materials must be submitted at least 7 working days before the relevant workshop. Post-workshop M E reports must be submitted within 5 working days after workshop completion. No specific application deadline is stated in the supplied information. Who Should Consider This Opportunity? This consultancy is particularly suited to established professionals who have already developed substantial experience in gender equality and facilitated learning or dialogue programmes. Potentially suitable candidates may include professionals working in: Gender equality Women s rights Human rights Social sciences International development Gender studies Community development Social norm change Male allyship Gender-transformative programming Training and facilitation Community engagement Advocacy Peace and development International development programmes However, applicants should carefully compare their qualifications with the stated requirements, particularly the 5-year professional experience requirement and the requirement for experience facilitating programmes related to gender equality, male allyship and equitable masculinities. Visit HERE learn more about the UN Women HeForShe Barbershop Facilitator Consultant Roster Conclusion The UN Women HeForShe Barbershop Facilitator Consultant Roster provides an opportunity for experienced gender equality and facilitation professionals to become part of a global pool of pre-vetted experts supporting the expansion of the Barbershop Toolkit. The programme focuses on engaging men and boys in conversations about gender equality, equitable masculinities and social norm change. Successful consultants may support the adaptation and delivery of sessions across different languages, cultures and communities. The consultancy is home-based and primarily remote , while short-term national or international travel may be required for particular assignments. Consultants will be expected to complete onboarding, adapt session materials, facilitate worksho s, conduct monitoring and evaluation, meet reporting deadlines and contribute to the wider Barbershop community of practice. The opportunity is best suited to professionals who already possess significant experience in gender equality-related facilitation. Applicants should have a relevant advanced degree or an accepted combination of a first-level degree and additional experience, at least five years of professional experience, demonstrated experience facilitating gender-related dialogue or training programmes, and fluency in English. Importantly, inclusion in the consultant roster does not guarantee employment or future assignments . Consultants are engaged according to UN Women s programme needs, partner requests and available resources. For qualified professionals with the appropriate background, the roster can provide an opportunity to contribute to a global initiative focused on challenging harmful gender norms and advancing more equitable approaches to masculinity.
